memories.content: Calculate user study compensation budgets based on estimated participation burden, combining session time and preparation effort.
Compensate for required travel time in face-to-face user studies as well.
Compensate for the actual time participants spent in sessions, regardless of research modality.
Leave cash payment as an available compensation method for face-to-face studies.
If compensation equity is explained, do not require finalizing the payment method at the proposal stage.
Apply the same base hourly rate to face-to-face and remote studies if task burden is equal.
Participants judge compensation fairness based on the total burden, combining session time with required travel and preparation time.
Account in compensation for the burden of rescheduling iterations and returning for multiple formative evaluation sessions.
Compensate participants for time already invested even if a session is terminated early due to prototype errors.
The author of this proposal tends to exclude preparation burden between sessions when calculating compensation for iterative studies.
Allow the problem framing to extend through a third sentence when a concrete person, setting, or use situation is needed to make the issue understandable.
Use the third sentence for the specific setting and consequence rather than compressing them into an abstract two-sentence summary.
Explicitly specify the users, operational stakeholders, and actual usage environment in the primary HCI research question.
Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
Present the master’s research schedule as phase-specific milestones for field understanding, system implementation, user study, and analysis.
Link deliverables that determine entry into the next phase to each milestone of the master’s research.
Directly connect the gap in the actual usage context with the proposed design and operational contributions in a single flow.
Avoid extra subheadings in a two-page proposal; use paragraph transitions to preserve one continuous argument from problem to proposed response and next steps.
Begin each paragraph by connecting it to the previous claim so the short proposal reads as an argument rather than a stack of labeled fragments.
Place preliminary results from field observations or technical validations near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
Readers may misinterpret a compressed opening when the person, setting, or consequence is only implied.
A two-sentence opening can become so general that readers understand the topic but cannot picture the situation the proposal intends to change.
Use paragraph transitions instead of extra headings when the repeated labels would consume space needed for the argument itself.
End each paragraph with the question or consequence that the next paragraph answers.
A continuous sequence of problem, consequence, response, and next step makes the relationship among claims audible without repeating section labels.
Readers may experience very short headed sections as an outline because each new label interrupts the connection to the previous paragraph.

analysis.overview: The frames address separate operational domains: participant-compensation policy versus concise HCI proposal construction. Neither side supplies a claim that semantically matches, qualifies, or contradicts one on the other side, so all substantive guidance remains independently useful one-sided information.
